prompt: In `READ COMMITTED`, when is the view of the data that a statement sees taken?

choices.text: When the transaction begins
choices.why: That is REPEATABLE READ, more exactly its first statement.

choices.text: When each statement starts
choices.why: Right: two SELECTs in one transaction can see different values if someone committed between them.

choices.text: When the row is first locked by the transaction, and never again after that
choices.why: Plain reads take no row locks; the view is per statement.

choices.text: At COMMIT
choices.why: A view taken at commit would be too late to read anything with.

prompt: Window B waited 5881 ms for window A's row lock and then still overwrote A's raise. Why did the wait not help?

choices.text: Window A had not committed yet when B wrote
choices.why: B's write went through only after A committed.

choices.text: READ COMMITTED does not take row locks
choices.why: It does; that is what B waited for.

choices.text: The value was a literal computed from a read made before the wait
choices.why: Right: B wrote 9390 from its own SELECT of 9290; re-reading the row after the wait cannot change a constant.

choices.text: psql cached the earlier result
choices.why: psql caches nothing; the application logic did.

prompt: Which of these `UPDATE`s is safe against the lost update in `READ COMMITTED`, with no other change?
hint: Where is the new value computed?

choices.text: `UPDATE products SET price_cents = 9390 WHERE id = 1` after reading 9290
choices.why: That is the lesson's lost update: the value comes from a stale read.

choices.text: `SET price_cents = price_cents + 100`
choices.why: Right: the arithmetic is done on the row the UPDATE finds after any wait, so both raises were kept, 9590.

choices.text: `SET price_cents = 9390` inside `BEGIN … COMMIT`
choices.why: The lesson's lost update was inside BEGIN … COMMIT; a transaction alone protects nothing it read.

choices.text: Any UPDATE that names the row by primary key
choices.why: All the lesson's updates used id = 1, including the lost one.

prompt: In the pgbench run under `READ COMMITTED`, how many of the price raises were lost?

An inventory service reads `stock`, checks that it is above zero in application code, and writes `stock - 1` as a number it computed. Under `READ COMMITTED`, what is the smallest change that makes it safe?
hint: The check needs the value, so it must be read.

choices.text: Raising the isolation level of the whole database to SERIALIZABLE
choices.why: It would catch it, but every transaction would then need retries; it is not the smallest change.

choices.text: Reading the stock with `SELECT … FOR UPDATE`
choices.why: Right: the second reader waits before reading and then sees the first one's change, like windows A and B with 9690.

choices.text: Running the read twice and comparing
choices.why: Both reads can happen before the other writer commits.

choices.text: Adding an index on stock
choices.why: An index changes how rows are found, not who sees whose changes.

prompt: What error does a `REPEATABLE READ` transaction get when it updates a row someone else changed after its snapshot?

choices.text: `deadlock detected`
choices.why: That is 40P01, two transactions waiting for each other.

choices.text: `could not obtain lock on row`
choices.why: That comes from NOWAIT, lesson 12.

choices.text: `could not serialize access due to concurrent update`
choices.why: Right: the transaction is refused rather than allowed to overwrite a change it never saw.

choices.text: `canceling statement due to lock timeout`
choices.why: That needs lock_timeout and is about waiting, not snapshots.

prompt: Window A's `REPEATABLE READ` transaction read 22090 twice, although window B had raised the price to 22190 in between. Why?

choices.text: Window B had not committed
choices.why: B's update ran outside a transaction and committed at once.

choices.text: A read from a cached copy in psql
choices.why: Each SELECT went to the server; the server answered from A's snapshot.

choices.text: B's change was rolled back
choices.why: It stayed: A's own UPDATE then failed because of it.

choices.text: Its snapshot was taken at its first query
choices.why: Right: every statement in the transaction reads from that one snapshot.

prompt: Under `REPEATABLE READ`, 28,848 pgbench transactions failed and the cents added equalled the committed count, 49,741. What does that show?

choices.text: No raise was lost; the losers were refused instead
choices.why: Right: a silent wrong answer became a loud failure, which a retry can then fix.

choices.text: The failed transactions were retried automatically by the server, so nothing was lost
choices.why: The server never retries; pgbench ran with one try each.

choices.text: REPEATABLE READ is slower than READ COMMITTED
choices.why: Speed is not what the two counts show, and rates moved a lot between runs.

choices.text: A third of the prices were not changed
choices.why: All ten prices changed; a third of the attempts were refused.

prompt: Reading the same row twice in one transaction and getting two different values is called a non-___ read.
hint: The name of the level that prevents it.

prompt: What does `SERIALIZABLE` promise about transactions that run at the same time?
hint: Compare with running them one at a time.

choices.text: That they never run concurrently
choices.why: They do run concurrently; that is what makes the level useful.

choices.text: A result some one-at-a-time order could produce
choices.why: Right: and when it cannot keep that promise, it fails one of them with 40001.

choices.text: That each sees every change the others commit as soon as they commit it
choices.why: That is closer to READ COMMITTED; SERIALIZABLE reads from a snapshot.

choices.text: That they wait for each other's row locks instead of failing
choices.why: It fails rather than waits its way out, as the 40001 showed.

prompt: Why did `REPEATABLE READ` let both of customer 7's pending orders in?
hint: Did either transaction write a row the other wrote?

choices.text: The count query did not use an index
choices.why: Indexes change speed, not what a snapshot shows.

choices.text: Window B committed before window A
choices.why: A committed first, and the order did not matter.

choices.text: Each inserted a new row, so nothing was overwritten
choices.why: Right: REPEATABLE READ refuses to overwrite a changed row; write skew writes different rows.

choices.text: Pending orders are not covered by isolation, because status is a text column
choices.why: Isolation applies to every column of every table.

prompt: A hospital requires at least one doctor on call. Two doctors, each in a `REPEATABLE READ` transaction, count the doctors on call, see two, and each sets their own row to off call. What happens, and what would have stopped it?

choices.text: One gets 40001 under REPEATABLE READ, so the rule holds
choices.why: They update different rows, so REPEATABLE READ has nothing to refuse.

choices.text: They deadlock, and the server cancels one
choices.why: Neither waits for the other: no row is wanted by both.

choices.text: Both commit and nobody is on call; SERIALIZABLE would refuse one
choices.why: Right: it is the lesson's write skew with updates instead of inserts.

choices.text: Nothing goes wrong, since both read the same count
choices.why: Reading the same stale count is exactly the problem.

prompt: For the one-pending-order rule, what does the lesson suggest instead of relying on `SERIALIZABLE`?

choices.text: A partial unique index on `customer_id` where `status = 'pending'`
choices.why: Right: the second insert fails with a unique violation at any isolation level.

choices.text: A table lock on orders in every checkout
choices.why: It would work by stopping every other order in the shop while one is placed.

choices.text: A longer deadlock_timeout
choices.why: There is no deadlock here to time.

choices.text: An advisory lock per customer
choices.why: It can work if every code path remembers it; the index cannot be forgotten.

prompt: Match each level to how it behaves when two transactions race over the same price.

pairs.right: both commit and one raise is lost
the loser runs again and both raises are kept

prompt: Which SQLSTATE codes does the lesson say are worth retrying?

choices.why: Right: a serialisation failure and a deadlock both mean the transaction lost a race and was rolled back whole.

choices.text: Every error the server returns
choices.why: A syntax error or a constraint violation fails the same way every time.

choices.text: 23505, the unique violation
choices.why: Retrying a duplicate key gets the same duplicate key.

choices.text: Only errors raised at COMMIT, not ones raised earlier in the transaction
choices.why: 40001 arrived at UPDATE under REPEATABLE READ and at COMMIT under SERIALIZABLE; both are retried.

prompt: Why does `bump.py` put the `SELECT` of the price inside the function the loop calls again, rather than reading once before the loop?

choices.text: psycopg requires every statement to be inside a function
choices.why: psycopg has no such rule.

choices.text: So that a retry starts from the new price
choices.why: Right: retrying only the write with the old price would be the lost update again.

choices.text: Reading inside a transaction is faster
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: SERIALIZABLE forbids reads outside transactions, so the read had to move inside
choices.why: A read outside would simply be its own one-statement transaction.

prompt: Two copies of `bump.py` made 500 raises each. By how many cents did product 1's price rise?
A checkout function charges the customer's card, then inserts the order, all inside one transaction wrapped in a retry loop. What goes wrong when the insert gets 40001?

choices.text: The retry fails again, since the error is permanent
choices.why: 40001 is the retryable kind; the order would very likely go in.

choices.text: The database rolls back the card charge
choices.why: The card charge happened outside the database, which cannot undo it.

choices.text: Nothing: the loop handles it
choices.why: The loop repeats everything inside it, including the side effect.

choices.text: The card is charged twice
choices.why: Right: side effects outside the database belong after the commit, never inside a retried transaction.

prompt: Put the steps of one retry loop iteration in order, as `bump.py` does them.
hint: The read is inside the transaction.
items: UPDATE to the price plus one
COMMIT, or catch 40001 and roll back
Wait a random, doubling time and start again
trap: The wait comes after the rollback: a transaction left open while sleeping would hold its locks the whole time.

prompt: Which statements about the three levels are true, according to this lesson's measurements? Choose all that apply.
hint: Look at the cents added, not the rates.

choices.text: READ COMMITTED reported no failures and still lost raises
choices.why: Right: 0 failed, 17,981 lost.

choices.text: Under REPEATABLE READ every committed raise was kept
choices.why: Right: 49,741 committed, 49,741 cents.

choices.text: SERIALIZABLE with retries committed almost every transaction it attempted
choices.why: Right: only 17 gave up after ten tries.

choices.text: SERIALIZABLE prevents conflicts from happening
choices.why: It detects them and fails a transaction; 20,781 retries were needed.

choices.text: The transaction rate is the reliable number for comparing the levels
choices.why: The lesson says the rates moved a lot between runs; the counts did not.
